ACUTE HEART FAILURE 
 
 
 
 
 
GENERAL APPROACH 
 
•
Clinical features: Dyspnoea, orthopnoea, effort intolerance, peripheral oedema, PND. Gallop rhythm, 
increased JVP, chest crackles, cardiac murmurs. 
•
ECG Features: AF, new T wave changes, LVH, LBBB.  Noncardiogenic pulm oedema: cerebral Twaves 
•
CXR: pulmonary oedema, pulmonary venous congestion, cardiomegaly, Kerley B lines 
•
Ultrasound features: > 3 B lines bilaterally, pleural effusions, poor contractility, dilated IVC 
 
•
Triage to RESUS AREA IF ACUTELY DISTRESSED OR UNSTABLE 
•
Rapid ABC assessment, IV line, monitors, HGT, VBG, urine ßHCG, ECG 
•
Correct electrolytes abnormalities 
•
Crystalloid fluid bolus 10 - 20mg/kg if hypotensive.  
PATIENTS ARE OFTEN INTRAVASCULARLY DEPLETED, DESPITE PERIPHERAL FLUID OVERLOAD 
•
Comprehensive history and exam, including: 
§
Onset, underlying risk factors, likely precipitant. NB prior CCF, ACS history 
§
Co-morbidities, chronic medications, compliance 
•
Document specific ECG changes, POCUS findings 
•
Further investigations: FBC, U&E, CXR, serial ECGs, troponin, proBNP if diagnosis in doubt 
•
Differential diagnosis: PE, LRTI, chronic lung disease, fluid overload from other causes e.g. renal/liver 
failure, non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema e.g. CVA, head injury, negative pressure oedema etc. 
DISPOSITION 
 
•
Cardiology consult 
•
Will likely require CCU/High care 
•
Continue serial ECG and VBG monitoring in ED 
TREATMENT OPTIONS 
 
•
Nitrocine: Vasodilator, decreases preload (and afterload 
at higher doses. 
§
1-2 mg IV boluses OR Infusion 30µg/min, max 
dose 150-200 µg/min. See infusion protocol 
§
Caution in preload dependent patients – RV 
infarction, pulmonary HT, aortic stenosis 
•
NIV: CPAP or BiPAP, more PEEP than pressure support. 
§
Significant reduction in intubation requirements 
if started early 
•
Furosemide (Lasix®): Diuresis, decreases fluid overload 
§
Patients daily dose as an IV bolus to start, or 20-
40mg IV if not on Lasix previously 
§
Caution in severe renal failure/anuria 
§
Consider infusion (discuss with cardiology) 
•
Inotropes: May be required for cardiogenic shock 
§
Dobutamine preferred – see infusion protocol 
§
May add adrenaline if poor response, sepsis 
 
FIND AND TREAT THE PRECIPITANT 
CAUSES 
•
Infection/Sepsis 
•
ACS – new or old ischaemia, RV infarct, VSD or ventricular wall rupture 
with tamponade 
•
Arrhythmias – AF common, fast AF may precipitate failure 
•
Uncontrolled Hypertension – HT emergency, HT cardiomyopathy 
•
Valvular pathology – new murmur may indicate acute mitral regurgitation, 
requires urgent surgery! 
•
Cardiomyopathy – Ischaemic, DCMO, alcoholic, pregnancy, RVD, HT etc. 
•
Endocrine – Thyrotoxicosis/myxoedema coma 
•
Myocarditis – recent viral illness 
•
Severe anaemia 
FIND AND TREAT THE UNDERLYING CAUSE! 
Dr du Plessis / Dr R Gihwala CMJAH Emergency Department June 2020
